industry: Home Services / Residential HVAC & Plumbing (PE-backed multi-branch rollup)
businessModel: Private-equity-backed buy-and-build rollup of residential HVAC, plumbing, and electrical service-and-replacement companies operating as a multi-branch platform
businessStage: Mid-rollup (platform + 6 bolt-on acquisitions), scaling toward a leveraged recapitalization
sourceNote: Real-world pattern from the PE-driven home-services consolidation wave (mirrors public patterns from platforms in the residential HVAC/plumbing rollup space such as the Wrench Group / Apex / Sila cohort and franchise-adjacent operators). Reflects the well-documented post-acquisition integration trap where consolidated revenue grows via M&A but same-branch operating metrics — technician billable utilization, dispatch efficiency, first-time-fix rate, and membership-plan attachment — deteriorate as branches run on disparate dispatch software and uneven scheduling discipline. Metrics reflect typical residential service-and-replacement KPIs (revenue per truck, billable utilization, callback rates).

ownerIntake.stage: Consolidated revenue $68M TTM, up 52% YoY — but almost all growth is acquired, not organic (organic same-branch revenue +3%). Technician billable utilization 58% (industry benchmark 70-75%). Net leverage 4.6x EBITDA; recap targeted in 12-15 months.
ownerIntake.ownerGoal: Restore consolidated EBITDA margin to 13%+ and revenue per truck to $450k+ within 12 months to support a leveraged recapitalization at a 9x+ EBITDA multiple.
ownerConstraints: Net leverage 4.6x EBITDA; the recap and the sponsor's return thesis depend on EBITDA-margin recovery within 12-15 months, not just more acquisitions.

Three of the six acquired branches still run their original, separate dispatch/field-service software (different from the platform's ServiceTitan instance); no unified scheduling or capacity view across branches.
Skilled-technician labor market is tight: average 9-week time-to-fill for a senior HVAC technician; cannot simply hire utilization up.

Membership/maintenance-plan attachment varies wildly by branch (platform branches 41% of customers on plans; two acquired branches under 12%), driving inconsistent recurring demand and winter/summer demand smoothing.
Seasonality: HVAC demand peaks in summer/winter; shoulder seasons show idle technician capacity, magnifying utilization gaps.
Integration team is thin (2 ops integration leads for 6 bolt-ons); branch managers retain significant autonomy per acquisition earn-out agreements running another 6-14 months.
ownerIntake.immediateConcern: Consolidated revenue is up 52% but EBITDA margin has fallen 350bps and revenue per truck dropped from $430k to $367k since the rollup began. The sponsor cannot tell whether the margin decline is dilution from buying lower-quality businesses, a pricing problem, or a post-acquisition operational integration failure. With the recap window opening in 12-15 months, the team must identify the highest-leverage fix before committing capital to either more acquisitions, a pricing overhaul, or a costly software migration.

businessProblem: A PE-backed residential home-services rollup has grown consolidated revenue 52% through acquisition while EBITDA margin fell 350bps and revenue per truck dropped from $430k to $367k. Organic same-branch revenue is nearly flat (+3%) and technician billable utilization sits at 58% versus a 70-75% benchmark. Management must determine whether the margin erosion is acquisition dilution (bought weaker businesses), a pricing/labor-rate problem, or a post-acquisition operational-integration failure in dispatching and capacity utilization — before deciding among more acquisitions, a pricing overhaul, or an expensive platform-wide dispatch-software migration, all under 4.6x leverage and active earn-out constraints.

evidence.finding: Technician billable utilization is 58% against a 70-75% industry benchmark, and revenue per truck fell from $430k pre-rollup to $367k (top-quartile operators reach ~$525k). The same trucks and technicians are producing materially less billable output post-rollup, indicating capacity is being lost in scheduling/dispatch rather than in demand or pricing.
evidence.source: Fleet and labor reporting, technician timecards, industry KPI benchmarks

evidence.finding: Three of six acquired branches still run their original, separate dispatch/field-service software, with no unified scheduling or cross-branch capacity view. There is no normalized branch-level KPI scorecard, so dispatch efficiency (jobs/tech/day, drive-time, idle hours) cannot be compared across branches. This is a structural integration gap that prevents the platform from balancing load and enforcing scheduling discipline.
evidence.source: IT systems inventory, integration team notes, ops review

evidence.finding: Consolidated revenue grew 52% YoY but organic same-branch revenue grew only 3%, while EBITDA margin fell from 13% to 9.5% (-350bps). Growth is almost entirely acquired, and profitability per dollar of revenue is deteriorating — the platform is getting bigger but less efficient, consistent with integration drag rather than healthy organic scaling.
evidence.source: Consolidated and segment financials, M&A contribution analysis

evidence.finding: Membership/maintenance-plan attachment varies extremely by branch: platform branches at 41% of customers, two acquired branches under 12%. Plan members provide recurring demand, demand-smoothing across shoulder seasons, and higher replacement-lead conversion. Low-attachment branches therefore have lumpier demand and lower utilization — but plan attachment is an operational discipline, not a demand-quality problem.
evidence.source: Membership program data by branch, recurring-revenue analysis
